UnitStatement: Large language models can draft engineering documents, extract scope dependencies, reconcile conflicting specifications, generate cost estimates, and produce analysis reports resembling competent engineering work.
The engineering-document capability of large language models is transformative.
Raw large-language-model capability is incompatible with regulated professional engineering practice.
The incompatibility is not merely that large language models sometimes produce bad output.
Large-language-model output carries no intrinsic epistemic warrant.
Correct and incorrect large-language-model claims are generated by the same mechanism.
Correct and incorrect large-language-model claims share surface properties of fluent prose, specific values, and confident tone.
Hallucination is the term of art, but the underlying phenomenon is deeper than that label.
A model output is not self-certifying.
A model output cannot be assumed grounded in evidence merely because it reads authoritatively.
Professional engineering practice is a duty-of-care regime.
A licensed professional who authenticates a professional work product accepts personal, non-delegable responsibility for its accuracy, completeness, and fitness for purpose.
Under Alberta engineering law and APEGA practice standards, authentication requires direct supervision and control or a thorough review.
Direct supervision and thorough review presuppose that the professional can assess the epistemic grounding of work-product claims.
A professional must be able to distinguish known claims from assumptions, extracted claims from inferences, and evidence-supported claims from unsupported claims.
Uncontrolled large-language-model output does not support professional assessment of epistemic grounding.
Authoritative-looking model text can lack provenance, epistemic labels, and evidence-to-interpolation boundaries.
Regulatory thorough review of uncontrolled model output becomes a complete independent re-derivation.
Complete independent re-derivation eliminates the productivity benefit of using artificial intelligence.
The thesis asks how systems engineering principles can govern LLM-based agent systems for reliance in regulated professional engineering practice.
The thesis response is to engineer governance architecture rather than to make the model more reliable.
The proposed governance architecture makes every claim epistemic status transparent and auditable.
Transparent and auditable claim status lets a qualified professional determine what to rely on.
Chirality is a formally specified agent operating system for deliverable-heavy professional work.
Chirality makes all project state live in git-tracked plain files.
Chirality uses no external database.
In Chirality, the filesystem is the single source of truth.
Filesystem-as-truth supports traceability, immutable snapshots, content-addressed approval, and the complete audit trail.
Chirality organizes agents into Type 0, Type 1, and Type 2 agents.
Type 0 Architect agents define invariant protocols and design standards.
Type 1 Manager agents orchestrate work through gate-controlled workflows with human authority at every decision junction.
Type 2 Specialist agents execute bounded tasks within declared write scopes and return auditable outputs.
Authority flows downward in the agent hierarchy.
Escalation flows upward in the agent hierarchy.
No agent type can bypass a human gate.
The architecture is governed by workflow design requirements R1-R9, decomposition invariants I1-I10, and system-wide invariants K-*.
The invariant layers are enforced through agent instructions, runtime orchestration, human gates, and deterministic tooling.
The system is implemented as a desktop application with an indexed agent suite, registered deterministic toolset, and formal governance document suite.
Active membership is maintained in source registries rather than mutable count prose.
The architecture is grounded in the APEGA regulatory framework through a professional practice standard.
The professional practice standard maps Chirality to requirements of the Relying on the Work of Others and Outsourcing practice standard.
The thesis claims five novel contributions.
The first contribution is an epistemic architecture for LLM reliability transparency.
Mandatory provenance, no-invention rules, conflict surfacing, and epistemic labeling make each system-produced claim transparent and auditable.
The system makes unsupported claims structurally visible rather than trying to prevent hallucination.
Existing approaches focus on reducing hallucination rates as a population-level improvement.
Professional practice requires per-claim epistemic transparency.
The second contribution is a regulatory mapping that grounds AI agent governance in existing professional obligations.
APEGA obligations can be interpreted to govern AI agent use because the professional obligations depend on what the professional must do, not what the worker is.
AI agent governance may be achievable within existing regulatory frameworks without new AI-specific regulation.
The regulatory-governance interpretation remains jurisdiction-dependent and regulator-dependent.
The third contribution is a four-pillar philosophical framework with fractal instantiation.
The architecture rests on ontology, epistemology, praxiology, and axiology.
The architecture identifies epistemology as the load-bearing pillar.
The epistemology has a formal ontology of six primitives: claim, warrant, status, gap, conflict, and ruling.
The warrant lifecycle is UNWARRANTED to CITED to REVIEWED to AUTHENTICATED.
The warrant lifecycle tracks the epistemic state of claims interleaved with the deliverable lifecycle.
The four pillars are presented as a compact framework for professional accountability, not as the only possible ontology for every domain.
The four-document production kit consists of Datasheet, Specification, Guidance, and Procedure.
The production kit mirrors the philosophical structure as a fractal property.
The fractal property is treated as evidence of architectural coherence within Chirality.
The fourth contribution is a fault containment architecture through write scope quarantine.
The Type 0, Type 1, and Type 2 hierarchy combined with declared write scopes creates formal fault containment zones.
A Type 2 agent failure cannot corrupt source truth.
Write-scope fault containment adapts classical systems-engineering fault containment to governance of probabilistic agents.
The fifth contribution is a three-layer invariant system with four-layer enforcement.
Thirty-nine formally stated invariants are enforced through agent instructions, runtime orchestration, human gates, and deterministic tooling.
The invariant system is a formal methods contribution applied to governance of LLM-based agent systems.
Chapter 2 surveys AI agent architectures, LLM reliability, formal methods and safety-critical systems engineering, professional regulation, and epistemic frameworks.
Chapter 2 identifies the literature gap that motivates the thesis.
Chapter 3 presents the four pillars, the load-bearing role of epistemology, and the fractal property.
Chapter 4 presents filesystem-as-state, entity model, lifecycle state machine, type hierarchy, write scope, invariant system, orchestration, and contracts.
Chapter 5 develops six epistemic primitives, four enforcement mechanisms, the warrant lifecycle, worked examples, and comparison to alternatives.
Chapter 6 presents the APEGA regulatory mapping and argues that AI agents are others under Section 3.0.
Chapter 7 examines the architecture through eight systems-engineering disciplines.
Chapter 8 presents the indexed agent suite, registered toolset, desktop application, and validation mechanisms.
Chapter 9 assesses limitations, generalizability, and future work.
Chapter 10 restates the contributions and answers the research question.
Appendix A provides the full invariant catalog.
The current agent index is maintained in AGENTS.md.
Appendix C provides the detailed APEGA regulatory mapping.
The thesis presents the architecture, philosophical foundation, regulatory grounding, and implementation.
The thesis does not present empirical validation through controlled studies with practicing engineers.
Controlled studies with practicing engineers are identified as the highest-priority future work.
The thesis does not present a regulatory ruling or endorsement by APEGA.
The regulatory mapping is the firm interpretation, not a regulator pronouncement.
The thesis does not claim that the architecture eliminates LLM hallucination.
The architecture makes LLM hallucination visible rather than absent.
The thesis does not claim that instruction-level enforcement is sufficient alone.
The architecture relies on multi-layer defense in depth.
The thesis contribution is architectural rather than empirical.
The thesis demonstrates that a professional-practice AI-agent governance architecture can be designed, specified, implemented, and grounded in existing regulation.
Whether the architecture improves professional review in measured practice remains a future empirical-study question.
